metadata.name: Home Prep
metadata.disclaimer: This information is general home preparedness guidance and is not a substitute for instructions from emergency officials, your utility companies or your doctor. When local officials give directions during an emergency, follow them.

entries.title: Storing Water
entries.summary: Store enough clean water for your household, in the right containers, and keep it fresh.
steps: Plan on at least 4 L (1 gallon) per person per day for drinking and basic hygiene. Store at least 3 days' worth, and 2 weeks' worth at home if you can.
Add more for nursing mothers, children, sick people, hot climates and pets.
Use food-grade containers made for water: unopened bottled water, or clean PETE (#1) or HDPE (#2) water jugs and barrels.
Clean reused containers with dish soap and water, then sanitize with 1 teaspoon of unscented bleach per liter (quart) of water. Swish, let stand 30 seconds, empty and air dry.
Fill them with tap water from a treated public supply; it needs nothing added. Well water or other sources should be disinfected first.
Seal the containers, label them with the date, and store them in a cool, dark place off the floor.
Replace home-filled water every 6 months. Keep commercially bottled water until its expiration date.
do_not: Do not reuse milk or juice jugs; they're hard to clean and break down over time.
Do not store water containers near gasoline, pesticides or other chemicals; vapors can pass through plastic.
Do not store all your water in one large container that you can't move or carry.
watch_for: Leaks, cloudiness or algae in stored water.
Weight: a 208 L (55 gal) barrel weighs about 208 kg (460 lb) full. Put it where it will stay and get a pump or siphon to draw from it.
notes: Mix sizes: large containers at home, and smaller jugs or bottles you can carry if you evacuate.
Your water heater, pipes and ice also hold water you can use in an emergency. See Emergency Water Sources at Home.

entries.title: Disinfecting Water at Home
entries.summary: Make water safe to drink by boiling it or treating it with household bleach in the right amount.
steps: If water is cloudy, let it settle, then filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter first.
Boiling is the most reliable method: bring water to a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft). Let it cool and store it in clean, covered containers.
If you can't boil, use plain, unscented liquid household bleach. Check the label for its strength (sodium hypochlorite percentage).
For 6% bleach, add 8 drops per 4 L (1 gallon), or 2 drops per liter (quart).
For 8.25% bleach, add 6 drops per 4 L (1 gallon), or 2 drops per liter (quart).
Double the dose if the water is still cloudy, colored or very cold after filtering.
Stir and wait at least 30 minutes. The water should have a slight chlorine smell. If not, repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes.
Improve the flat taste of boiled water by pouring it back and forth between clean containers.
do_not: Do not use scented, color-safe, splash-less or bleach with added cleaners.
Do not expect boiling or bleach to remove chemicals, fuel, heavy metals or salt.
Do not use water that smells of fuel or chemicals, even after treatment.
watch_for: Old bleach, which loses strength over time. Use bleach less than about a year old.
Boil-water notices from your water utility. Use treated water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, washing dishes and making ice.
notes: Water purification tablets and portable filters also work; follow their package instructions.
Floodwater may contain chemicals that no home treatment removes. Use stored water instead whenever possible.

entries.title: Emergency Water Sources at Home
entries.summary: Find the hidden water already in your home when the taps stop, and protect it from contamination.
steps: If officials report contamination of the public water supply, close your home's main water valve right away so dirty water doesn't enter your pipes and water heater.
Water heater: turn off the power or gas first, close the cold-water inlet valve at the top, open the drain valve at the bottom, and open a hot-water tap in the house to let air in.
Let the first water from the water heater run out until sediment clears, then collect the rest in clean containers.
Pipes: open the highest faucet in the house to let air in, then collect water from the lowest faucet.
Use melted ice cubes, and the liquid in canned fruits and vegetables.
Toilet tank water (not the bowl) can be used if it doesn't contain colored cleaners or tablets. Disinfect it before drinking.
Treat any water you're unsure of by boiling or with bleach. See Disinfecting Water at Home.
do_not: Do not turn the water heater's power or gas back on until the tank is full again; an empty tank can be damaged or start a fire.
Do not drink water from swimming pools, hot tubs or waterbeds; use it for flushing toilets and cleaning only.
Do not use water from radiators or heating systems.
watch_for: Hot water from the water heater; let it cool before draining.
Water that collected after the supply was contaminated; disinfect it before drinking.
notes: A typical water heater holds 150 to 300 L (40 to 80 gal).
Learn where your main water shutoff is now. See Shutting Off Utilities.

entries.title: Food Safety When the Power Fails
entries.summary: Keep refrigerated and frozen food cold as long as possible, and know what to throw out.
steps: Keep the refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible.
A closed refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours. A full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.
Put appliance thermometers in the refrigerator and freezer before an emergency so you can check temperatures without guessing.
If the outage will last longer than 4 hours, move perishables into coolers packed with ice or frozen gel packs.
Use dry ice for a long outage if you can get it; handle it with gloves and keep the room ventilated.
Throw out perishable food such as meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, soft cheese and leftovers that has been above 4 °C (40 °F) for more than 2 hours.
Frozen food that still has ice crystals or is at 4 °C (40 °F) or below can be refrozen or cooked.
do_not: Do not taste food to decide whether it's safe; spoiled food can look and smell normal.
Do not store dry ice in a closed space where people sleep, or touch it with bare hands.
Do not put food outside in the snow; sun and animals can make it unsafe.
watch_for: Insulin and refrigerated medicines; see Medications and Medical Needs.
Food that touched floodwater, which must be thrown out unless it's in sealed metal cans that can be cleaned.
notes: Keep frozen water bottles in the freezer; they fill empty space, keep it cold longer and become drinking water.
When in doubt, throw it out.

entries.title: Building and Rotating a Food Supply
entries.summary: Build a supply of food your household will actually eat, store it well and use it before it expires.
steps: Start with at least 3 days of food for everyone, and build toward 2 weeks or more.
Store what you already eat: canned meats, fish, beans, soups, vegetables and fruit; peanut butter; rice, pasta and oats; crackers; dried fruit and nuts.
Choose foods that need little water or cooking, and include comfort foods.
Plan for special needs: infant formula, allergies, medical diets and pet food.
Store food in a cool, dry, dark place, ideally below 21 °C (70 °F), off the floor and in sealed containers to keep pests out.
Rotate: put new purchases at the back and use the oldest first.
Check dates every 6 months, and eat or donate food before it expires.
Keep a manual can opener and basic utensils with the supply.
do_not: Do not store food in a garage, attic or car where temperatures swing widely.
Do not stock up on foods nobody in the household likes; they won't get rotated.
Do not eat from cans that are bulging, leaking, deeply dented along a seam or badly rusted.
watch_for: Salty foods, which increase how much water you need.
Pests such as weevils, mice and moths in grains.
notes: Pantry tracks what you have and when it expires, and the Depletion Calculator shows how long it will last.
An adult typically needs around 2,000 calories a day, more when working hard or in the cold.

entries.title: Cooking Without Power
entries.summary: Cook and heat food safely during an outage, and use less fuel doing it.
steps: Use grills, camp stoves and propane burners outdoors only, away from doors, windows and vents.
Indoors, cook only with appliances made for indoor use, such as a fireplace or wood stove that vents to a chimney.
Plan some no-cook meals: canned food can be eaten cold, and sandwiches, cereal and fruit need no heat.
Save fuel: use lids, cut food into small pieces, soak beans and pasta first, and turn off the heat early and let food finish in the hot pot.
Retained-heat cooking: bring food to a boil, then wrap the covered pot in blankets or put it in an insulated cooler to finish cooking.
Keep a fire extinguisher and a pot lid nearby to smother small grease fires.
do_not: Do not use a charcoal or gas grill, camp stove or generator indoors, in a garage or on an enclosed porch.
Do not use a gas oven or range to heat your home.
Do not leave cooking unattended.
watch_for: Signs of carbon monoxide poisoning: headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion. Get everyone into fresh air.
Fire hazards near grills and stoves: overhanging branches, fences and dry grass.
notes: Store extra propane tanks outdoors, upright and away from the house.
A thermos keeps water hot for hours after one boil.

entries.title: Getting Through a Power Outage
entries.summary: Keep light, communications and essential devices running through a long outage, and stay safe while you do.
steps: Use flashlights and battery lanterns for light, not candles.
Unplug sensitive electronics and appliances to protect them from a surge when power returns. Leave one lamp switched on so you know when it's back.
Save phone battery: lower screen brightness, close apps, and turn on low-power mode. Charge phones from power banks or a car outside.
Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for news.
If someone depends on powered medical equipment, have a backup power plan, and know where to go if it runs out.
Check on neighbors, especially older people and those living alone.
Report the outage to your utility, and treat traffic lights that are out as all-way stops.
do_not: Do not go near downed power lines; stay at least 10 m (33 ft) away and assume they're live.
Do not run a car in an attached garage, even with the door open, to charge devices or stay warm.
Do not open the refrigerator and freezer more than you must.
watch_for: Heat or cold in the house; see Staying Warm Without Power and Staying Cool Without Power.
Fire from candles, space heaters and overloaded extension cords.
notes: Device Status shows your phone's battery and how long it may last.
Keep spare batteries and charged power banks with your emergency supplies, and rotate them.

entries.title: Generator Safety
entries.summary: Run a portable generator without poisoning your household, electrocuting anyone or starting a fire.
steps: Run the generator outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from the house, with the exhaust pointing away from doors, windows and vents.
Install battery-powered carbon monoxide alarms near sleeping areas and test them.
Set it on a dry, level surface, sheltered from rain under an open canopy, never in water or on wet ground.
Plug appliances into the generator directly, with heavy-duty outdoor extension cords rated for the load.
Add up the wattage of what you'll run, including the extra startup surge of motors such as refrigerators and pumps, and stay under the generator's rating.
Turn off the generator and let it cool before refueling.
Store fuel in approved containers away from the house and any flame, and add stabilizer for long-term storage.
do_not: Do not run a generator inside a home, garage, basement, crawl space or shed, even with doors and windows open.
Do not plug a generator into a wall outlet to power the house (backfeeding). It can electrocute utility workers and neighbors. Have an electrician install a transfer switch.
Do not refuel a hot or running generator.
watch_for: Headache, dizziness, nausea or tiredness indoors while the generator runs. Get everyone into fresh air and call for help.
Damaged or frayed cords, and cords running under rugs or through water.
notes: Run the generator for a while every few months so it starts when you need it.
Many carbon monoxide deaths after storms come from generators. Placement is what keeps you safe.

entries.title: Staying Warm Without Power
entries.summary: Keep your household warm through a winter outage without risking fire or carbon monoxide.
steps: Pick one small room, ideally on the sunny side and away from outside walls, and gather everyone there.
Close doors to other rooms, and hang blankets over doorways and windows. Open curtains on sunny windows by day and close them at night.
Wear layers, a hat and socks, and use sleeping bags and blankets. Sleeping together in one room helps.
Eat regular meals and drink warm fluids; your body burns food for heat.
Use only heaters rated for indoor use, follow their ventilation instructions, and keep a carbon monoxide alarm nearby.
A fireplace or wood stove that vents to a chimney is a safe heat source; open the damper first.
Prevent frozen pipes: let cold-water taps drip and open cabinet doors under sinks.
If it gets too cold to stay safely, go to a warming center or a friend's home.
do_not: Do not heat your home with an oven, gas range, grill, camp stove or generator.
Do not leave space heaters unattended or near curtains and bedding.
Do not use a fireplace whose chimney hasn't been inspected.
watch_for: Hypothermia in older adults, infants and anyone sick: shivering, confusion, drowsiness, slurred speech.
Burst pipes when the heat comes back. Know where your main water shutoff is.
notes: A tent set up indoors and covered with blankets holds body heat well.
Hot water bottles in sleeping bags add warmth for hours.

entries.title: Staying Cool Without Power
entries.summary: Get through a heat wave with no air conditioning, and spot heat illness before it becomes an emergency.
steps: Close blinds and curtains on sunny windows during the day.
Open windows at night and early morning to let cooler air through, especially on opposite sides of the house.
Stay on the lowest floor, where it's coolest.
Drink water regularly, even if you're not thirsty, and avoid alcohol and heavy meals.
Cool your body: take cool showers or baths, and put damp cloths on your neck, wrists and armpits.
Do heavy work in the early morning or evening, and rest in the shade during the hottest hours.
Go to a cooling center, library or other air-conditioned place if you can, especially during the hottest part of the day.
Check on older neighbors, infants, people with chronic illness and pets at least twice a day.
do_not: Do not rely on a fan alone when it's very hot; once the air is hotter than about 35 °C (95 °F), fans can't prevent heat illness.
Do not leave anyone, including pets, in a parked car.
watch_for: Heavy sweating, weakness, headache, nausea and cramps: heat exhaustion. Move to a cooler place and cool down.
Confusion, fainting, or hot skin with little sweat: heat stroke. Call emergency services and cool the person immediately.
Medications that make heat illness more likely; ask a doctor or pharmacist.
notes: The Extreme Heat Wave scenario card covers the first hours and days.
Heat kills more people in the US than any other kind of weather.

entries.title: Toilets and Sanitation When the Water's Off
entries.summary: Deal with human waste safely when toilets won't flush, and keep the household from getting sick.
steps: If the sewer works but the water is off, flush by pouring a bucket of water (about 4 to 8 L, or 1 to 2 gallons) quickly into the bowl. Use water you can't drink, such as bath or pool water.
If the sewer may be broken, as after an earthquake or flood, don't flush at all.
Make an emergency toilet: line a sturdy bucket with two heavy-duty trash bags, or line the empty toilet bowl the same way.
After each use, cover waste with a scoop of cat litter, sawdust, shredded paper or dry soil to absorb liquid and cut odor. Keep the lid on.
When a bag is no more than half full, tie it shut and put it in a covered trash can or container outside, away from water and living areas, until it can be collected.
Set up a handwashing station near the toilet: a jug of water with a spigot, soap and a bucket to catch the water.
Clean toilet areas and surfaces regularly with a bleach solution, about 80 ml (1/3 cup) of bleach per 4 L (1 gallon) of water.
do_not: Do not bury waste near wells, gardens or water you might drink.
Do not put bags of waste in with regular household trash without checking local guidance.
Do not skip handwashing; diarrhea spreads fast in households without running water.
watch_for: Diarrhea or vomiting in the household. Keep the sick person's toilet separate if you can.
Sewage backing up into drains, which means the sewer is damaged. Stop using any water that goes down a drain.
notes: Keep an emergency toilet kit ready: a bucket with a lid, heavy-duty bags, absorbent material, toilet paper, gloves, hand sanitizer and bleach.
Using separate containers for urine and feces reduces odor and the volume of waste you need to store.

entries.title: Building a Go-Bag
entries.summary: Pack a bag for each person with what you'd need to leave home in minutes and get by for several days.
steps: Pack one bag per person, light enough for them to carry. Keep bags near the door or in the car.
Water and food: water for at least a day plus a way to treat more, and 3 days of food that needs no cooking.
Health: a first aid kit, a 7-day supply of medications, spare glasses or contacts, and hygiene items.
Light and communication: flashlight or headlamp, extra batteries, a battery-powered or hand-crank radio, a phone charger and power bank.
Documents: copies of IDs, insurance, prescriptions and important contacts in a waterproof bag, plus cash in small bills.
Clothing: a change of clothes, warm layers, rain gear and sturdy shoes.
Tools: multitool, whistle, N95 masks, duct tape, local paper map, and work gloves.
Add what's specific to your household: infant supplies, pet food and leashes, mobility aids, a comfort item for children.
Check the bags every 6 months: replace expired food, water, medicine and batteries, and update clothing for the season.
do_not: Do not pack so much that you can't carry the bag a long distance.
Do not keep the only copy of important documents in the bag.
watch_for: Children who've outgrown clothes and shoes in their bag.
Heat in a car trunk, which spoils food, medicine and batteries faster.
notes: Turn this list into a Checklist so you can tick items off as you pack and review.
Your Emergency Planner holds contacts and rally points that pair with the go-bag.

entries.title: Making a Household Emergency Plan
entries.summary: Decide ahead of time how your household will reach each other, where you'll meet and how you'll leave.
steps: Choose an out-of-area contact everyone will call or text to check in. Long-distance connections often work when local ones are jammed.
Pick two meeting places: one just outside your home, and one outside your neighborhood in case you can't get home.
Plan two evacuation routes out of your area in different directions, and know where you would go.
Find out the emergency plans at work, schools and child care, and who is allowed to pick up children.
Plan for anyone who needs extra help: older relatives, people with disabilities, and pets.
Write contacts down on paper as well as in your phone, and give each person a copy.
Practice the plan at least once a year, including a home fire drill and driving the evacuation routes.
do_not: Do not rely on calling during a disaster; text messages often get through when calls don't.
Do not assume everyone will be home when something happens.
watch_for: Plans that only one person knows. Make sure everyone, including children, knows the basics.
Out-of-date phone numbers and changes in schools or work.
notes: The Emergency Planner stores contacts, rally points and your communication plan, all available offline.

entries.title: Shutting Off Utilities
entries.summary: Know where your gas, water and electricity shutoffs are, and when and how to turn them off.
steps: Find and label your gas meter valve, main water shutoff and electrical panel now, before an emergency.
Gas: shut it off only if you smell gas, hear hissing, or officials tell you to. Use a wrench to turn the valve a quarter turn so it runs crosswise to the pipe.
If you smell gas, get everyone out first, then shut off the gas from outside if you can do it safely, and call the gas company from away from the building.
Water: turn the main valve clockwise to close it when a pipe bursts, or when officials report the water supply is contaminated.
Electricity: switch off the individual circuit breakers first, then the main breaker. To restore power, turn on the main first, then the circuits one at a time.
Keep a wrench tied near the gas meter, and show every adult in the household where the shutoffs are.
do_not: Do not turn the gas back on yourself; once it's off, only the gas company should restore it and relight pilot lights.
Do not touch the electrical panel if you're standing in water or the area is wet. Call an electrician or the utility.
Do not use light switches, phones or anything that could spark inside a building that smells of gas.
watch_for: A meter that's still spinning or a hissing sound after shutting the gas off; leave and call for help.
Water damage near the panel or appliances after a flood; have them checked before using them.
notes: Some homes have automatic seismic or excess-flow gas shutoff valves; know whether yours does.
Turning off gas unnecessarily can leave you without heat for days while you wait for the utility.

entries.title: Medications and Medical Needs
entries.summary: Keep medicines and medical supplies going through an emergency, including insulin and powered devices.
steps: Keep a written list of everyone's medications, doses, allergies, conditions and doctors, in your go-bag and wallet.
Build a reserve of at least 7 days of prescription medicines, and more if your doctor and pharmacy allow early refills.
Store medicines in a cool, dry place and rotate them so the reserve stays in date.
Insulin in vials or cartridges, opened or not, can be kept unrefrigerated between 15 and 30 °C (59 to 86 °F) for up to 28 days. Check your product's label; some differ.
Keep insulin and other refrigerated medicines out of direct heat and sunlight, in an insulated bag with cool packs if possible, without letting them freeze.
For powered medical devices, keep backup batteries charged, know how long they last, and register with your utility's medical priority program if it has one.
Keep extra over-the-counter basics: pain relievers, antihistamines, anti-diarrhea medicine and oral rehydration salts.
do_not: Do not use medicines that got wet in floodwater; replace them.
Do not use insulin that has frozen or looks cloudy when it should be clear.
Do not use oxygen near open flames, candles or a gas stove.
watch_for: Running low on medicine during a long emergency. Contact a pharmacy early; many areas allow emergency refills during declared disasters.
Signs of illness getting worse without regular medication, such as high or low blood sugar or breathing trouble.
notes: Ask your pharmacist which of your medicines are temperature-sensitive.
Keep a cooler and gel packs in the freezer for moving medicines quickly in an outage.
